stories.headline: Captive-Bred Broad-Headed Snakes Released Into the Wild in a World First, With at Least Four Surviving
stories.summary: Six captive-bred juvenile broad-headed snakes were released into restored habitat in New South Wales in May, and at least four have survived the first months. It is the first wild release of the endangered species anywhere, and artificial rocks designed to mimic natural shelter are helping them.
stories.narrative:
In mid-May, researchers in New South Wales released six young, captive-bred broad-headed snakes into carefully restored habitat. It is the first time this endangered Australian species has ever been returned to the wild from captivity.

The effort is led by Professor Jonathan Webb of the University of Technology Sydney, working with the conservation group Aussie Ark and traditional owners of the Shoalhaven region. Indigenous rangers have been trained to help monitor the animals. The breeding program began in October 2024 and has produced eight snakes so far, with two kept back for their genetics.

The species badly needed help. Webb's thirty-four-year study in Morton National Park found the population dropped by about two thirds by 2023, after drought, the 2020 bushfires, and the removal of bush rocks that young snakes use for shelter and hunting.

To replace those hiding places, biologist Benjamin Croak designed artificial rocks with crevices of the right size and the right thermal properties. They keep juveniles warm and safe from predators such as kookaburras, cats and foxes, and they attract the lizards the snakes eat. The team checks the snakes every two weeks.

The good news is that at least four of the six have made it through the first few months. The snakes take about five years to mature, so it will be a long road before breeding is confirmed. But the team plans more habitat work and more releases over the coming years, and it is a real step forward for a species that has been sliding toward extinction.

stories.headline: Sikhs and Hindus Help Rebuild Punjab Mosques Destroyed After Partition
stories.summary: In Indian Punjab, Sikh and Hindu villagers are donating land, money and labour to rebuild mosques lost since Partition. Whole villages of all faiths are contributing, and new mosques have been opened with shared feasts.
stories.narrative:
In villages across the Indian state of Punjab, Sikhs and Hindus are helping to rebuild mosques that were destroyed or abandoned after the partition of India and Pakistan in 1947.

In Jakhiwal, a 77-year-old Sikh woman, Bibi Rajinder Kaur, urged her grandson to donate land so the village could have a mosque again. In Punawal, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a Hindu priestly family, gave land for a new mosque, which was finished in February. He then hosted a feast for the whole village, and people of every faith chipped in money, bricks and cement.

In Umarpura, local Sikhs helped restore an old Muslim shrine, with one man donating his own labour. He described the local mood as one of love and unity.

Many of those leading the work are old enough to remember the violence of Partition, which makes the gesture especially moving. It is a concrete example of neighbours repairing, with their own hands, something that was broken generations ago.

stories.headline: Terns Return to Pagham Harbour Colony Wiped Out by Avian Flu, With 756 Sandwich Terns Nesting Again
stories.summary: A south-coast England seabird colony abandoned after the 2022 avian flu outbreak now hosts 756 Sandwich terns, plus rising numbers of little terns, ringed plovers and oystercatchers. RSPB staff credit years of predator-proofing, habitat management and visitor education.
stories.narrative:
On the south coast of England, a seabird colony that was emptied by bird flu three years ago is full of life again.

Pagham Harbour, between Brighton and Southampton, lost its Sandwich tern colony after the 2022 avian influenza outbreak swept through. The birds simply stopped nesting there, and for a while it looked as though the site might stay silent.

The RSPB, the UK's bird conservation charity, kept working anyway. Staff and volunteers put up predator-proof fencing to protect ground-nesting birds, watched for rats, and cleared vegetation selectively so the birds had open ground to nest on. Rangers and volunteers also patrolled the shoreline, talking with visitors about how easily walkers and dogs can disturb nests, and dog-friendly areas were set up away from the colony.

The payoff has been striking. Sandwich tern numbers have gone from zero to 756 nesting birds. Little terns, ringed plovers, black-headed gulls and oystercatchers have all increased as well. The RSPB's senior project manager, Wez Smith, says the site is now thriving, with record-breaking populations using it.

The colony is part of the wider Solent Seascape project, which covers around 128,000 acres of coastal habitat. It's a hopeful reminder that even after a disease outbreak devastates a colony, careful, patient site management can bring birds back.

stories.headline: Venomous Primate Feared Extinct for 100 Years Found Alive on Indonesia's Bangka Island
stories.summary: The Bangka slow loris, one of the world's few venomous primates and once listed as possibly extinct, has been confirmed still living on Bangka Island. A local rescue centre's records, which show more than 90 animals rescued and 86 released since 2015, revealed it was there all along.
stories.narrative:
A small, big-eyed primate that scientists feared might be gone has turned out to be alive and well.

The Bangka slow loris is one of the very few primates in the world that is venomous. It produces a toxin from glands on its upper arms and mixes it with saliva, so its bite can damage tissue. Western science had not documented it since the 1930s, and by 2015 it was considered possibly extinct.

A 2022 field guide first hinted that the animal still existed on Bangka Island in Indonesia. Now Austrian scientists and international colleagues have published a paper confirming it, and the key evidence came from a local organisation, the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center.

Between 2015 and 2025, Alobi rescued more than 90 of the lorises, usually after they wandered into gardens, plantations or roads, and released 86 back into the wild. Those records suggest the species is probably more widely spread across the island than anyone thought.

Conservation group Re:wild points out that the discovery shows how much conservation depends on the knowledge of local communities. It's a rediscovery that offers a real chance to protect a species before it is lost.

stories.headline: Drones and AI Help Tongariro National Park Recover One Year After Destructive Fires
stories.summary: A year after fires burned about 3000 hectares and closed the Tongariro Crossing, red tussock and flax are regrowing. DOC, iwi and a Rotorua firm are using drones and AI to find weeds like gorse and broom so crews can target them precisely.
stories.narrative:
A year after fire tore through Tongariro National Park, the land is healing, and some clever technology is helping it along.

The first blaze burned about 3000 hectares of tussock grassland and regenerating alpine scrub, and closed the Tongariro Crossing for more than a week. A smaller fire a month later added to the damage. Both were sparked by vehicle faults.

DOC rangers say natural regrowth is well underway, with red tussock and flax returning, although larger celery pines were killed. A ten-year rāhui from Ngāti Hikairo ki Tongariro protects the burned land, helping keep out invasive weeds.

The biggest threat to recovery is weeds such as gorse, broom and heather, which love bare ground. Rather than combing whole blocks by helicopter, DOC now uses drones and an AI platform from Rotorua company Interpine to identify weed patches, so crews can go straight to them. Three large aerial surveys have been flown, with another planned for December. The government has put $3.5 million toward the recovery, and iwi contractors have been used where possible.

It's a good example of local effort and modern tools working together to bring a national treasure back.

stories.headline: Dunedin Marae Night Markets Bring Hangi, Free Health Checks and Community Together
stories.summary: Āraiteuru Marae in Dunedin runs monthly night markets, the first at a southern marae, drawing 300-400 people to its first one. Alongside food stalls and a talent quest, visitors can get free, confidential sexual-health tests.
stories.narrative:
In Dunedin, a marae has turned the last Friday of the month into a community event.

Āraiteuru Marae on Shetland Street runs night markets, an idea borrowed from Auckland and the first of their kind at a southern marae. Manager Tania Sharee Williams says the aim is to bring people together and help them meet neighbours they would never otherwise meet. The first market in September drew 300 to 400 people.

Stalls sell hangi-style lamb and chicken, plus Fijian, Tongan, Afghani, Palestinian and Cambodian food, and local businesses sell crafts inside the marae buildings. A health service also offers confidential advice and free finger-prick hepatitis C tests, along with quick HIV and syphilis tests, in a setting that feels far less intimidating than a doctor's office.

Some markets have also let residents meet parliamentary candidates. A talent quest on November 27 is open to all ages, and the final market of the year is on December 11. The marae, which depends on volunteers, also uses the income to keep its doors open.

stories.headline: Study Finds Species Down to Fewer Than 50 Individuals Can Recover When Conservationists Step In
stories.summary: A review of 141 bird and mammal species that fell below 50 wild individuals found that 61% of those given direct conservation help recovered to at least 100. The finding challenges the idea that tiny populations are doomed.
stories.narrative:
A new study from Monash University and the Zoological Society of London offers some of the most encouraging evidence yet that species on the very edge of extinction can come back.

The researchers looked at every bird and mammal known to have dropped below fifty wild individuals since 1950. Of those, 141 had histories documented well enough to analyse. Then they asked a simple question: what happened to the ones that got help, and what happened to the ones that didn't?

The answer was stark. Among fifty-one species that received direct conservation action, about sixty-one percent climbed back to at least a hundred individuals. Among species with no direct support, thirty-seven percent went extinct, and only two percent reached a hundred.

The most successful approach combined tackling the threat, such as controlling invasive predators or restoring habitat, with hands-on management of the population itself, through captive breeding or moving animals to new sites. One example is the Lord Howe woodhen, an Australian bird that dwindled to just twenty-three individuals in the late 1970s and now numbers more than sixteen hundred.

Lead author Dr Donal Smith argues the results show that being small isn't itself a death sentence. For anyone following efforts like New Zealand's predator control and species translocations, it is a hopeful, data-backed sign that the work pays off, even for the most precarious species.

stories.headline: Woman Becomes First Person to Swim the Entire California Coastline
stories.summary: Long-distance swimmer Catherine Breed covered about 900 miles of California's coast in 111 days, from the Oregon border to the Mexican border. She says no one had attempted the route before, and she did it through storms, big waves and a hostile current.
stories.narrative:
A long-distance swimmer named Catherine Breed has finished a swim that, by her account, nobody had tried before: the whole length of the California coastline, roughly 900 miles, completed in 111 days.

She set off on the first of July from the Oregon-California border and came ashore on a pier on the nineteenth of October, escorted throughout by a support boat. At the southern end she swam more than three miles offshore as she crossed the Mexican border, so she could stay clear of pollution coming out of the Tijuana River.

The plan had taken three years of preparation and aimed for about ten miles a day over ninety days. The sea had other ideas. A strong El Niño season brought tropical storms, waves as high as seven feet, and a warm current running north against her. She had eight encounters with sharks, and also swam alongside sea lions, dolphins and whales.

Breed already had a serious open-water record, including the English Channel, the North Channel, and swims from San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge to Half Moon Bay and out to the Farallon Islands. This was a far longer undertaking than any of those.

She says she wants the swim to encourage other people, especially women and girls, to chase goals that look impossibly big. It is a feat of patience and stubbornness, and a reminder of what steady daily effort can add up to.

stories.headline: Brazil Expands Pantanal Matogrossense National Park by More Than a Quarter
stories.summary: Brazilian authorities have enlarged Pantanal Matogrossense National Park by about 185 square miles. The addition protects wildlife corridors in the world's largest flooded grassland, home to the densest concentration of jaguars on Earth.
stories.narrative:
Brazil has made one of its most important wetland parks bigger. Pantanal Matogrossense National Park, which covered about 523 square miles, has been expanded by roughly 185 square miles, an area comparable to Redwood National Park in the United States.

The Pantanal is the largest flooded grassland in the world, and it is extraordinarily rich in life. It supports hundreds of bird and fish species, well over a hundred kinds of reptiles and amphibians, and mammals such as giant otters, giant anteaters, giant armadillos, tapirs and the highest concentration of jaguars anywhere.

The conservation agency that manages the park identified biological corridors that animals use to move in and out of it, and the expansion helps secure them. Those corridors matter because they keep populations connected and genetically healthy, which is especially important for endangered species. Keeping them open will depend on cooperation with local landowners.

The wetland has faced serious fires and droughts in recent years, and protecting the rivers that feed it helps the land hold on to water. Local reporting described the expansion as meeting a long-standing demand from scientists and environmentalists, which makes this a concrete gain rather than a promise.

stories.headline: Philippine Village Uses Bamboo, Oyster Shells and Coconut Husks to Hold Back Floods
stories.summary: In Pamarawan, a fishing village on Manila Bay, a nature-based sea defence built mostly by villagers has reportedly kept floods away for almost two years. It cost about $2 million and is trapping sediment where mangroves can be replanted.
stories.narrative:
In the low-lying fishing village of Pamarawan, in Bulacan province north of Manila, residents have been protected from flooding by something unusual: bamboo, oyster shells and coconut husks rather than concrete.

The project, the first of its kind in the Philippines, was designed by a Dutch engineering firm and approved in 2023, with work starting in 2024. Bamboo cribs cover about 14 hectares of shoreline, and oyster shells packed into coconut-husk nets help slow waves and trap sediment. The whole thing cost around 130 million pesos, reportedly less than a conventional sea wall.

Villagers did most of the work. The firm says between 80 and 90 percent of the construction labour came from the community of about 3,000 people.

Residents report no flooding for almost two years, and a local councilor said the village escaped this year's floods that hit neighbouring areas. Those are local accounts rather than independent measurements. Mud has already built up by about a foot in places, and mangroves could be planted there within a couple of years, restoring habitat that Bulacan lost heavily in past decades.

There are caveats: some fish-corral operators lost income, and not all were compensated. Still, the public works department has praised the pilot as something that could be replicated elsewhere, though the engineers say each site needs its own design.

stories.headline: Botswana Villages Earn Money From Camera-Trap Photos of the Wildlife They Live Alongside
stories.summary: In two remote villages on the edge of the Okavango Delta, residents are paid for each species their camera traps capture, with elephants earning the most. The Harmony with Wildlife scheme gives communities a tangible reward for tolerating crop-raiding and livestock-killing animals.
stories.narrative:
On the edge of Botswana's Okavango Delta, life alongside elephants, hippos and big predators means crops get raided and livestock gets killed. Two remote villages, Gogomoga and Tsutsubega, each with fewer than five hundred people and no paved roads, shops or electricity, are now being paid for the wildlife they put up with.

The scheme is called Harmony with Wildlife, run by the conservation nonprofit Wild Impact and the safari company &Beyond. Residents set up camera traps around their villages, and rangers check them weekly. Each species earns a different payment, and elephants earn the most. Every three months the money goes into an account held in the community's name, and villagers decide together how to spend it.

The idea grew out of work that began in April 2024, when community rangers started helping residents document wildlife damage so they could claim compensation from the government. After two years of footage, Wild Impact built an incentive model to reward the communities for their role in conservation.

This year's payments total about 57,600 pula, roughly four thousand US dollars. That is deliberately modest because the nonprofit funds it directly rather than relying on donors. Payments for the first two quarters of 2026 have reached the villages, and residents have met to discuss how to use them. An outside conservation planning professor says that if communities are expected to share land with wildlife, they need a tangible benefit, and this scheme provides one.

stories.headline: Pemba Fishers Help Create Two Community-Managed Marine Protected Areas Covering 1,300 km²
stories.summary: After catches fell, fishers on Pemba Island, Zanzibar, led the push for two new co-managed marine protected areas, officially gazetted in June 2026. Patrols have risen by over 50% and illegal fishing is reported down about 45%, and some fishers already report higher incomes.
stories.narrative:
On the east coast of Pemba Island, off Tanzania, fishers watched their catches shrink for years. The fisheries committee in Tumbe village assessed the decline themselves and took the findings to their neighbours. Many were hesitant, worried about losing income, but the community went on to ask the government for protection.

The result is two new marine protected areas, the North-East and South-East conservation areas, covering about 1,300 square kilometres. They are co-managed with more than twenty local communities, the Tanzanian fisheries authorities and several conservation groups. The government announced them at the UN Ocean Conference in June 2025 and they were officially gazetted in June 2026.

The rules include no-take zones, seasonal closures during spawning, and bans on spear guns and destructive nets, enforced through village by-laws. Women make up around thirty percent of fishery committee membership. According to one of the partner groups, patrols have risen by over fifty percent and illegal activity has fallen by about forty-five percent, though the article does not say how those figures were measured.

Officials say it is too early for hard evidence that ecosystems are recovering, and closures are tough for people who relied on year-round fishing. Even so, committee member Omar Hamad Salim credits better catches and living conditions, mangrove planting is under way, and new livelihoods such as premium fish sales and seaweed drying are being developed. It is a strong example of conservation led from the village up.

stories.headline: Kāpiti Council Votes to Restore Protection of Waikanae Urupā After 56 Years
stories.summary: Kāpiti Coast District Council has voted to restore Kārewarewa Urupā, a Māori burial ground, to the District Plan as a site of significance to Māori. The protection was removed in 1970 and an earlier attempt to restore it was quashed by the High Court.
stories.narrative:
After 56 years, a Māori burial ground in Waikanae is set to have its legal protection restored. Kāpiti Coast District Council has voted to add Kārewarewa Urupā to the District Plan as a site of significance to Māori, a change known as Proposed Plan Change 3.

The urupā is tied to the 1839 Battle of Kūititanga, and many of those killed were buried there. It has been used as a burial ground since the mid-1800s, but through Crown actions the iwi lost ownership and control, and its designation as a Māori cemetery was removed in 1970. About half the area was later built over with housing, and further development largely stalled after the remains of eleven people were uncovered in the early 2000s.

The council had tried to restore protections before, but that attempt was quashed by the High Court after a challenge from the landowner, the Waikanae Land Company. This time the council started a new process in 2024, and the iwi, Ātiawa ki Whakarongotai, presented its case with the help of resource management expert Dr Mahina-a-rangi Baker.

The undeveloped land gets a high level of protection, while the already developed area gets a moderate level. Existing residents can stay in their homes, and some development remains possible if ground disturbance is kept low and discovery protocols are followed. Dr Baker described it as an intergenerational fight to respect the basic human decency of the iwi's people. The decision can still be appealed to the Environment Court.

stories.headline: Māori Education Pioneer Graham Hingangaroa Smith Awarded Royal Society Research Excellence Medal
stories.summary: Distinguished Professor Graham Hingangaroa Smith has received the Te Puāwaitanga Research Excellence Medal from the Royal Society Te Apārangi for his work on Kaupapa Māori Theory. His four decades of work helped drive the growth of Kura Kaupapa Māori schools.
stories.narrative:
Distinguished Professor Graham Hingangaroa Smith, one of the leading figures in Māori education, has been honoured with the Te Puāwaitanga Research Excellence Medal at the Royal Society Te Apārangi Awards. The medal recognises his work developing and analysing Kaupapa Māori Theory, which has reshaped education in kura and universities in New Zealand and overseas.

Smith has spent more than forty years validating and advocating for Māori education systems. He told RNZ's Saturday Morning that being recognised by his peers meant a lot, though he credited others for much of his success.

His own schooling, at St Stephen's in Auckland and then through state schools, was in his words an ordeal, because it was so culturally different from home and aimed at assimilation. That experience shaped his later research.

He was involved early in the Kōhanga Reo movement. When children from the language nests moved into state classrooms, they quickly lost the Māori they had gained, and that prompted his group to start the Kaupapa Māori movement, giving Kōhanga graduates a real schooling option. He went on to help drive political change including the Education Act 1989, which greatly expanded Kura Kaupapa Māori, schools that had started outside the state system and struggled before they were accepted.

stories.headline: Support Dog Alerts Deaf Owner After Husband's Fall Down the Stairs, Saving His Life
stories.summary: Storm, a hearing support dog in Staffordshire, woke her deaf owner Sandra Donally just after midnight when husband Gary fell down the stairs. Sandra found him unconscious and bleeding, and believes he would not have been found until morning without the alert.
stories.narrative:
In Staffordshire, England, a support dog called Storm has been credited with saving a man's life. Sandra Donally, who is sixty-two, lost her hearing suddenly in 2017 because of a rare disorder, and was partnered with Storm in 2024.

Shortly after midnight, Sandra's husband Gary got up to use the bathroom, missed the handrail and fell down the stairs. Sandra could not hear any of it. Storm, however, jumped onto the bed and sat rigidly, staring toward the landing until Sandra got up to look.

She found Gary crumpled at the bottom of the stairs, unconscious and bleeding. Sandra believes that without Storm's alert she would not have discovered him until about half past six in the morning.

Gary had a broken jaw and spent twenty-four days at Royal Stoke Hospital while surgeons reconstructed it. He has survived, and Sandra says she will always be grateful to Storm for alerting her.

stories.headline: Two 'Unmusterable' Sheep Rescued From Te Mata Peak and Given Life-Saving Haircuts
stories.summary: Two sheep that had roamed Hawke's Bay's Te Mata Peak for months, weighed down by enormous fleeces, were finally caught by a team of SPCA and MPI staff, a farmer and his dogs. An ex-shearer volunteered to shear them, and they are in good health and heading to a new home.
stories.narrative:
High on the steep slopes of Te Mata Peak in Hawke's Bay, two sheep had been living wild for months, and their wool had grown so thick that from a distance they looked like clouds with their feet hidden. Earlier attempts to catch them had failed, and they had been described as unmusterable.

With summer approaching, the worry was heat exhaustion, because a sheep carrying that much wool in a Hawke's Bay heatwave is in real danger. So the Napier SPCA and an inspector from the Ministry for Primary Industries organised a rescue crew of six people and three dogs.

The key was a local farmer who knew the terrain. He climbed above the sheep and drove them down toward the waiting team. One was tackled by the MPI inspector, and the other simply sat down and let itself be caught, which SPCA inspector Jade Van Syp said made the whole thing far easier than anyone had expected.

The animals were tied, then lifted into a horse float with four people helping for each one. A retired shearer volunteered his time to take the fleeces off while SPCA staff steadied the sheep, and the wool came away quickly. Underneath, the sheep were in good health, a little overweight, and the wool was clean close to the skin.

The fleece is going to a local wool business that plans to make products from it, and the farmer who helped with the capture is adopting both sheep. It is a small story, but it shows an agency, a volunteer and a neighbour pulling together to save two animals that most people had given up on.

stories.headline: Dunedin Students' Strobe Light Keeps Nesting Birds Out of Tractor Engines
stories.summary: Four Year 13 students from St Hilda's Collegiate invented a strobe device that deters birds from nesting under tractor bonnets, a problem behind about $1.2 million in fire claims a year. Twenty-five are already on farms, and the team won Otago's Young Enterprise Company of the Year.
stories.narrative:
Four Year 13 students at St Hilda's Collegiate in Dunedin have come up with a practical fix for a costly farm problem: birds building nests in tractor engines. Alia Ryan, Neve Crossan, Bonnie Turner and Lucia Russell all come from rural backgrounds and had seen the problem first-hand.

Dry nesting material in a warm engine bay can easily catch fire, and starlings, whose breeding season runs from September to December, can build a nest very quickly. The insurer FMG says nesting birds cause about 1.2 million dollars in tractor fire claims every year, and they were linked to around a third of one hundred such claims over the past three years.

The students' answer is a strobe light that fits under the bonnet and deters birds from settling there. They built it through the Young Enterprise Scheme with help from an electronics company director, and according to Ryan nothing quite like it is on the market. Twenty-five devices are now running on farms in the region, with positive early feedback.

The team has won the 2026 Young Enterprise Otago Company of the Year award and will represent Otago at the national final in Wellington in December. They hope to keep the business going after they leave school. Meanwhile, FMG still advises farmers to stop and pop the bonnet to check before starting work.

stories.headline: Beavers Approved for Return to Loch Ness After 500 Years
stories.summary: NatureScot has licensed two charities to release up to 15 beaver families in the River Ness catchment over three years. Beavers were last recorded there in the 1500s, and more than 73% of consultation respondents backed the plan.
stories.narrative:
Beavers are going home to Loch Ness. Scotland's conservation agency NatureScot announced on October 30 that it has granted a licence to the charities Trees for Life and the Beaver Trust to release up to fifteen beaver families into the River Ness catchment over the next three years. The animals were last recorded there roughly five hundred years ago, in the 1520s.

Beavers are known as ecosystem engineers. Their dams create ponds and wetlands, which hold water back during floods, keep it available in droughts, and give a home to fish, amphibians, insects and birds. NatureScot's assessment found they could significantly boost biodiversity in the area, with a low risk of harm.

Most of the animals will come from other parts of Scotland where beavers are causing problems on prime farmland or are not settling well. Moving them rather than culling them is part of the appeal. Translocations could begin within weeks.

The plan had broad backing, with more than 73 percent of people responding to the consultation in favour. Some land managers and residents did raise concerns, and the agency says these will be handled through monitoring by the charities and its existing Beaver Mitigation Scheme. Beavers have been living wild in Scotland since a reintroduction in 2009 and have been steadily reclaiming old waterways.

stories.headline: Melbourne Police Officer With Ultra-Rare Blood Donates at All 85 Blood Centres in Australia
stories.summary: Trevor Bergman, one of about 150 Australians with the anti-D antibody, toured the country to give at every Lifeblood donation centre, reaching 545 donations in total. His blood is used to protect newborns from haemolytic disease.
stories.narrative:
Trevor Bergman, a 59-year-old police officer from Melbourne, has just finished a unique journey: donating blood at every one of Australia's 85 donation centres. His blood carries the anti-D antibody, which makes him one of only about 150 people in the country able to give it.

That antibody is used to protect babies. It is given to pregnant women whose immune systems could otherwise attack the blood of their developing child, a condition called haemolytic disease of the newborn. Donors like Bergman are genuinely scarce, so each donation matters.

The idea for the tour came to him on holiday in Perth. He then travelled the east coast, Western Australia and up to Darwin, giving at each stop. His most memorable visit was in Albany, where he was turned away because he had a sniffle. His 545th and final donation was in Canberra, where the Governor-General, Sam Mostyn, gave blood alongside him.

Lifeblood says one in three Australians will need donated blood at some point in their lives. Bergman's trip is a reminder of how much a single regular donor can do.

stories.headline: Derelict Kāpiti Convent Becomes a Thriving Co-Housing Village
stories.summary: A couple bought the long-vandalised former Marycrest boarding school near Ōtaki in 2016 and turned it into Makahuri, a co-housing village with residents from babies to 90-year-olds. It has shared gardens, a recycling station and a chapel used for events, and is part of a carbon forest project.
stories.narrative:
South of Ōtaki, on the Kāpiti Coast, a building that sat empty and vandalised for about seven years has become a village. Marycrest was once a Catholic girls' boarding school, closed in the early 1980s. In 2016 Drew Mackenzie and Anthony Ryan bought the 14.6 hectare property and set about bringing it back to life.

They replaced around two thousand windows and converted the buildings into homes and shared spaces, based on the co-housing model that began in Denmark in the 1960s. Today Makahuri has residents from under one year old to ninety, including students, retirees, families and full-time workers. They share a community garden, a recycling station run by resident John, and the old chapel, which hosts events and exercise classes and displays quilts made by resident Berylla Jones.

Mackenzie says it is a village rather than a commune, and that dealing with regulators meant repeatedly stressing that it is not a subdivision. The aim is about fourteen households, either buying apartments or renting. Newcomers are invited to working bees and a Friday morning café to see whether they fit.

The land is also part of the Ōtaki Carbon Forest Project, with paddocks being planted. It is a hopeful example of old buildings and new neighbours giving each other a second life.

stories.headline: DOC Whale Rescue Teams Free Humpback and First-Ever Southern Right Whale From Fishing Gear
stories.summary: New Zealand's Department of Conservation keeps two trained teams ready to cut entangled whales free. Recent rescues include a humpback near Kaikōura freed after more than 18 hours and the first recorded disentanglement of a southern right whale in Aotearoa.
stories.narrative:
A whale caught in fishing rope is in real trouble. It can be held in one place and slowly starve, and the rope can cut deep and become infected. Freeing an animal of around forty tonnes is dangerous work, so New Zealand's Department of Conservation trains and maintains two dedicated disentanglement teams.

RNZ's Our Changing World programme joined the South Island team lead, Zac Penman, aboard a DOC boat off Kaikōura. The town is a good place to spot problems early, because humpbacks pass by on their migration and some young ones now stay all year. Boats, planes and helicopters are always watching, so alerts tend to come quickly.

A rescue starts with finding the whale and attaching a satellite tracking buoy. Then comes careful planning, because choosing which rope to cut first matters enormously. Penman likens it to defusing a bomb. Three crew are needed: a skipper, a cutter with a long-handled hooked blade, and someone steadying the cutter. They work only from boats, following international guidelines written after a Kaikōura man was killed trying to help a whale in the water.

Recent results are encouraging. A humpback tangled in a crayfish pot line south of Kaikōura was freed after more than eighteen hours of work. In June the team freed a southern right whale caught in craypot lines off Rakiura Stewart Island, the first time one has been successfully disentangled in New Zealand.

The teams get only about six calls a year, and Penman has been involved in two successful rescues since taking the role. As he puts it, nothing makes you feel as good as saving a whale.

stories.headline: Southland's Tulip Open Day Draws Thousands and Raises Money for Local Groups
stories.summary: A Dutch-owned bulb grower donates tulip bulbs each year so an Edendale church and local clubs can raise funds at a festival that began in a farm shed in 2004. Thousands now come, including many from Southland's Indian and Filipino communities.
stories.narrative:
In Edendale, Southland, a farm shed event that began in 2004 has grown into one of the region's favourite days out. This year's Tulip Open Day, held on Labour Day, drew thousands of visitors, some travelling from as far as Auckland and Dunedin.

It works because of a simple act of generosity. The Dutch family company Triflor donates bulbs, and Edendale Presbyterian Church sells them as a fundraiser. The idea started when the church wanted money for a new kitchen, and a member suggested the bulbs. Other local groups raise funds on the day too, including the Men's Shed, the Lions club, the athletics club and the Wyndham museum.

Visitors can tour the tulip fields by minivan, walk the flowering headlands, and browse around forty food trucks and craft stalls. They can also order from eighteen varieties of bulb, delivered in March ready for planting.

The day has become a meeting place for Southland's multicultural community, with many Indian and Filipino health professionals among the crowds. Triflor, founded in the Netherlands in 1965, has grown bulbs around Edendale since 1991 and exports tens of millions each year, but its local manager says it wants to keep backing the community around it.

stories.headline: Kites and Looming-Eye Buoys Cut Seabird Deaths in Cornish Fishing Nets
stories.summary: A 17-month trial with ten Cornish fishers found kites cut the odds of catching guillemots and razorbills by 71%, and spinning eye buoys by 59%. Cheap deterrents could help reduce seabird bycatch in gillnets.
stories.narrative:
Gillnets kill tens of thousands of seabirds each year in European waters, so a simple, low-cost fix would be a big deal. A new study off Cornwall suggests there may be one.

Researchers from the University of Exeter worked with ten Cornish fishers over about seventeen months. Between late 2023 and early 2025 the fishers set more than a thousand camera-monitored nets, adding either bird-of-prey-shaped kites or spinning buoys with large looming eyes to some of them.

The results were clear. Nets with kites had 71 percent lower odds of catching auks, the group that includes guillemots and razorbills, which made up nearly three quarters of the unwanted catch. Nets with the looming-eye buoys had 59 percent lower odds.

There are caveats. Kites worked poorly in very light or very strong wind, and the buoys may attract seals. A separate Danish study found the buoy effect faded after about a month. Some authors work for a company that makes the buoys. Still, because fishers took part and the devices are cheap, the approach looks practical.

stories.headline: Rare Arnhem Sheath-Tailed Bat Detected 400 Miles From Its Last Known Home
stories.summary: A scientist at Australian Wildlife Conservancy picked up the call of a microbat rarely recorded since 1979, far from where it was last seen. The find will help researchers work out where the species lives and how to protect it.
stories.narrative:
Australia has a new clue about one of its most elusive bats. The Arnhem Sheath-tailed Bat was first identified in 1979 and has hardly been recorded since, partly because it is fast and lives in remote country.

Scientist Oli Aylen was surveying wildlife at the Pungalina-Seven Emu sanctuary, run by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy, when his handheld detector picked up unusual calls from bats flying over mangroves. One call was strangely short for its frequency, and he suspected it belonged to this species. It turned up about four hundred miles from where it was last known.

Nobody yet knows whether the bat is naturally uncommon, threatened, or simply under-recorded. The conservancy will now make it a priority in upcoming surveys, aiming to detect it by several methods, and ideally to find where it roosts.

As Aylen says, the more we know, the better we can protect them.

stories.headline: Azores Island Switches Off Streetlights Each October to Guide Young Seabirds to Sea
stories.summary: Corvo, a small Azores island, turns off public lighting for five nights so Cory's shearwater chicks aren't lured off course. More than 30,000 fledglings have been rescued across the Azores since 2015.
stories.narrative:
Each October, the small Portuguese island of Corvo in the Azores goes dark on purpose. For the last five nights of the month, public lighting is switched off from nine in the evening until four in the morning.

The reason is the Cory's shearwater. The Azores hold most of the world's breeding population, and young birds leave their nests at night to fly to sea. Town lights confuse them, and they end up grounded on land where they are vulnerable.

The island's 400 or so residents are on board; a survey of 207 of them found unanimous support. The scheme is run with the Portuguese Society for the Study of Birds. Volunteers also gather stranded chicks, often in cardboard boxes, and release them toward the sea.

According to The Guardian, more than 30,000 fledglings have been rescued across the Azores since 2015, about 6,000 of them on Corvo. Organisers hope other towns will follow, and a similar blackout was held on Madeira.

stories.headline: Over Half of Young Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Reach Remission in Diet and Exercise Trial
stories.summary: In a randomised trial of 96 adults aged 18 to 45, 54% on a supervised low-calorie diet and exercise programme were in remission at six months, versus about 4% on usual care. Longer-term results are still unknown.
stories.narrative:
A randomised trial from the University of Leicester and McGill University suggests that younger adults with type 2 diabetes can often put it into remission with intensive lifestyle support.

The study enrolled 96 adults aged 18 to 45 in England and Canada, all with type 2 diabetes and obesity. Fifty followed a programme of 800 to 900 calories a day, starting with meal replacements, plus supervised exercise twice weekly. Their diabetes and blood pressure medicines were stopped under medical supervision. The other 46 received usual care.

After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 in the programme, or 54 percent, were in remission, with blood sugar below the diabetes threshold and no glucose-lowering drugs. In the usual-care group, only two of 46 were. The programme group also lost about seven kilos more, mostly fat, and kept their muscle.

There are limits: the trial was small, open-label and only six months long, and remission is not a cure. Most side effects were mild, such as headaches and constipation. The authors want longer studies, but it is a hopeful result for a group often diagnosed young.

stories.headline: Satellite Tags Reveal the Northland and Auckland Harbours Where Green Sea Turtles Feed
stories.summary: Satellite tracking has shown which New Zealand harbours green sea turtles favour, from Rangaunu Bay to the Manukau. The DOC-led Team Turtle project can now follow the animals without disturbing them, and the data will help protect their habitat.
stories.narrative:
New Zealand scientists have been using satellite tags to find out where green sea turtles spend their time in local waters, and the first results are in.

The work is led by Dr Karen Middlemiss, a marine science advisor at the Department of Conservation, as part of a project called Team Turtle. The tags send location data to a constellation of satellites, so researchers can follow each turtle from a distance without disturbing its routine.

The turtles do not breed in New Zealand. Instead they treat our harbours as feeding grounds, a bit like a babysitting service for teenagers, as Middlemiss put it, before heading across the Pacific to breed. The favourite spots turn out to be Rangaunu Bay and Harbour, Pārengarenga Harbour, Whangārei Harbour and the Bay of Islands in Northland, plus the Manukau Harbour in Auckland.

Some individual stories stand out. One turtle swam from Northland down to Wellington and back, and another stayed a month in the Manukau. Many stay put in one harbour for long stretches.

Kelly Tarlton's, which has rehabilitated eleven rescued turtles, and Auckland Zoo's vets, who have treated eight sick ones since June, are partners in the effort. Knowing where the turtles gather helps target protection, and DOC is asking boaties to keep a lookout, fit propeller guards and slow down where turtles are common. Good information about where these animals live is the first step to keeping them safe.

stories.headline: High School Fills Entire Football Field With Groceries to Replenish New Jersey Food Banks
stories.summary: Students at Howell High School in New Jersey collected over a quarter of a million pounds of food in the second 100-Yard Food Drive Challenge. It was delivered to 30 food banks, the largest drive in the organiser's history.
stories.narrative:
Thousands of yellow donation bags covered the football field at Howell High School in New Jersey this autumn, stretching from one end zone to the other.

The bags were the result of the second annual 100-Yard Food Drive Challenge, run by a nonprofit called Dermer Dreams. Hundreds of students collected groceries in their neighbourhoods, and the football team and volunteers then loaded everything onto rented trucks.

In total, more than a quarter of a million pounds of food was gathered, the biggest drive the group has ever run. It was shared among about thirty food banks, including Lunch Break, Fulfill, the Howell Food Bank and Open Door in Freehold.

Dermer Dreams was founded in 2019 by Dan and Alyse Dermer, and its neighbourhood captain programme gives students a way to earn community service hours while tackling hunger. The first challenge took place last year at another high school, and this second edition was far larger. As Dan Dermer said, the students did more than collect food, they brought their communities together.

stories.headline: Vitamin B5 Supplement Pantethine Eases Psoriasis Symptoms in Early Trial
stories.summary: Chinese researchers found that pantethine, a vitamin B5 derivative, prevented psoriasis in mice and improved symptoms in a 12-week trial of 24 patients. It is early, proof-of-concept work, but it points to a cheap, widely available add-on treatment.
stories.narrative:
Researchers at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing have found a promising lead for treating psoriasis, a long-term skin condition with no cure.

The team, publishing in the Journal of Experimental Medicine, looked at pantethine, a form of vitamin B5 that is sold as a cholesterol supplement. They found that in people with psoriasis, enzymes called Vanins are unusually active in immune cells, using up pantethine and tipping the cells into overdrive. Topping pantethine back up reversed that effect.

In mice, pantethine prevented psoriasis from developing. In a small trial, 24 patients all used an ointment and half also took pantethine tablets. After twelve weeks the pantethine group had improved symptoms, especially those who began with higher cholesterol.

The authors call the results encouraging but preliminary. Larger trials are needed, but because pantethine is already widely available, the idea could move quickly if it holds up.

stories.headline: Charity Crowdfunds Millions to Buy 3,800-Hectare Rothbury Estate for Nature
stories.summary: The Wildlife Trusts raised about £30 million, including from 25,000 individual donors, to buy England's largest land purchase in three decades. The Northumberland moorland and forest will become a wildlife sanctuary and corridor.
stories.narrative:
A conservation charity in England has pulled off one of the country's biggest land purchases for nature. The Wildlife Trusts have bought the whole Rothbury Estate in Northumberland, some 3,800 hectares of moorland and forest that the Percy family, the Dukes of Northumberland, had held for almost eight centuries.

The money came largely from ordinary people. Around 25,000 individuals gave toward the land cost, and together with a National Lottery Heritage Fund grant of five million pounds and a government contribution, the campaign raised roughly thirty million pounds. Naturalist David Attenborough lent his support. The family had put the estate on the market in 2023 and gave the charity two years to find the funds.

The land was used for grouse shooting until 2022. The Wildlife Trusts plan to turn it into a biodiversity sanctuary, linking with neighbouring reserves to form a wildlife corridor of about 65 kilometres running inland from the North Sea. Species that could benefit include cuckoos, butterflies, pine martens, golden eagles and red squirrels.

The charity also wants to work with the dozen or so local farmers, mostly sheep keepers, to cut back on pesticides and chemical fertiliser. Britain is well short of its goal of protecting thirty percent of land and sea for nature by 2030, and the charity says this purchase is a meaningful step toward it.

stories.headline: Texas School District Names New Elementary After Beloved Custodian 'Miss Marilyn'
stories.summary: Aubrey ISD surprised 76-year-old Marilyn Hampton, a custodian for 39 years, by naming its new K-5 school Marilyn Hampton Elementary. She was told she was attending a meeting about opening challenges.
stories.narrative:
In Aubrey, Texas, a school district has honoured a woman who spent nearly four decades keeping its buildings running. Marilyn Hampton, known to everyone as Miss Marilyn, is 76 and worked 39 years as a custodian for Aubrey Independent School District. The district's brand new kindergarten-to-fifth-grade school will carry her name.

Hampton thought she had been invited to a board meeting to talk about the challenges of opening the new building. Instead she was asked to walk a red carpet with the school's name stitched into it. She cried and told the room how much they meant to her.

By all accounts she went well beyond her job. She bought school supplies, tutored students and ran the football ticket booth. She was the first of her seven siblings to graduate high school, and she still works with infants and toddlers at the district's early learning centre. The superintendent said she is truly Aubrey ISD.

It is a lovely reminder that the people who quietly hold a community together can be recognised while they are still there to enjoy it.

stories.headline: London's Oxford Street Goes Car-Free Along Nearly a Kilometre
stories.summary: Since 26 October, vehicles have been banned from the stretch between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street. It is the first step in a redesign with trees, seating and two new public squares.
stories.narrative:
One of the world's best-known shopping streets has become a place for walking. From 26 October, London's Oxford Street has been closed to cars, buses and bicycles along almost a kilometre, between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street.

The change is the first stage of a wider redesign that includes tree planting, seating and two new public squares. Mayor Sadiq Khan called it a new era for the street. Emergency vehicles keep access, and cleaning and refuse collection continue at set times.

The early days brought queues on neighbouring roads as buses were diverted, and the current set-up is a trial. Testing and review will carry on into spring 2027, with work on a permanent scheme later that year. Still, shoppers and visitors now have a calmer, cleaner street, and the move marks a real shift toward people-first city centres.

stories.headline: Shell by Shell, Volunteers Help Tara-iti Fairy Terns Recover Toward 50 Birds
stories.summary: At Bream Bay, volunteers and DOC staff build shell nesting patches and hand-rear early eggs, roughly doubling fledglings per season. The population, once down to three or four breeding pairs, is about 45 birds and the researcher hopes for 50 within a year.
stories.narrative:
New Zealand's rarest breeding bird, the tara-iti or fairy tern, is slowly climbing back. At Bream Bay north of Auckland, volunteers and Department of Conservation staff build sand-and-shell nesting patches placed away from storm tides and close to estuaries where young birds can learn to fish.

The approach is working. Fewer nests are lost since the patches began, and collecting early eggs to be hand-reared at Auckland Zoo, while the parents lay again, has roughly doubled productivity for those pairs. Fledglings have risen from about six a season to twelve, and in one year as many as eighteen or nineteen.

The population crashed to just three or four breeding pairs in the 1980s and now stands at about 45 birds. The lead researcher hopes it could reach around 50 within a year. Predators still take a third of eggs and chicks, so daily nest checks, trapping and fencing continue, with the local hapū Patuharakeke Te Taiao involved. A captive-raised female may breed this season, and the team is considering a new site north of Ruakākā.

stories.headline: Russell Nears Becoming the First Pest-Free Town on Mainland New Zealand
stories.summary: Volunteers in Northland's Russell have spent more than 20 years trapping rats, possums and stoats, and the town is now close to being declared pest-free. Kiwi and weka now live among the houses.
stories.narrative:
In the Bay of Islands, the small town of Russell is on the verge of a first for mainland New Zealand: becoming a pest-free town. The Russell Landcare Trust, which is largely run by volunteers, has spent more than twenty years removing introduced predators from the peninsula.

The scale of the effort is striking. About 7,500 traps and 10,500 bait stations cover roughly 3,000 hectares. Around 2,000 hectares are now free of possums and 1,000 hectares free of rats. In the town itself, the trust catches about one rat a month even with a trap every 25 metres, and the rubbish tip, once a reliable source of rats, has gone more than three months without a catch.

The wildlife is responding. Roughly 2,500 kiwi live on the peninsula, about three times the town's human population. Residents report kiwi and weka around their homes, and at one holiday park seven kiwi, four of them juveniles, were seen in a single evening. The park even removed the televisions from its cabins to encourage guests to look outside. Weka, which vanished locally around 1940, were reintroduced in 2002 and are doing well.

Landowners cooperate almost without exception, granting access for pest control 98 percent of the time when asked. New funding from Foundation North, the regional council and the Department of Conservation will help expand the buffer zone. The trust will keep watching for reinvasion, and hopes one day to bring back kōkako. As one longtime volunteer put it, the dawn chorus is now almost deafening.

stories.headline: Fernbird Returns to Wellington Region for the First Time in About 70 Years
stories.summary: A mātātā (fernbird) has been found at the Parangarehu Lakes in East Harbour Regional Park, where the species hasn't been recorded in roughly 70 years. Wetland restoration and predator control appear to have brought the birds back on their own.
stories.narrative:
A secretive native wetland bird has been found in the Wellington region for the first time in around seven decades. The mātātā, or fernbird, turned up during a baseline survey at Lake Kōhangaterā, also known as the Parangarehu Lakes, in East Harbour Regional Park.

Fernbirds are hard to spot. They hide in dense wetland vegetation, eat insects and small invertebrates, and are poor flyers, which made the discovery a surprise. Apart from a few small populations on Wellington's west coast, they have been absent from the lower North Island for about seventy years.

What makes the story especially pleasing is that nobody put them there. Taranaki Whānui had only recently been discussing whether to reintroduce the species, and the survey showed the birds had already come back by themselves. Bird surveyor Shane Cotter called the find significant for both the species and the park.

Greater Wellington's Jack Mace credited the combined work of the council, iwi and volunteers in restoring wetlands and controlling introduced predators. Officials say it is a sign that the work is paying off, and a reason to keep protecting the park and others like it across the region.

stories.headline: No Rats Found in Raukūmara Forest Block Where Kiwi Live After Iwi-Led Pest Control
stories.summary: A Ngāti Porou, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui and DOC restoration project on the East Cape found rat numbers fell from 80 percent to zero in a monitored area after an August operation. A trail camera captured a kiwi shortly after.
stories.narrative:
On the East Cape, the Raukūmara Pae Maunga Restoration Project has reported that rats have vanished from a large block of the Raukūmara Range where a small population of kiwi lives.

The project is a partnership between Ngāti Porou, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui and the Department of Conservation, backed by 34.4 million dollars in government funding from 2020. The conservation park spans 250,000 hectares, the largest continuous native forest left in the North Island, which had suffered from generations of deer, pigs and goats stripping the understory.

After an aerial operation in August covering nearly 50,000 hectares, tracking tunnels in one monitored area showed rat numbers dropping from 80 percent to zero. A trail camera caught a kiwi soon afterwards, and the birds were present both before and after the operation.

Locals have been central. Trustee Ora Barlow said the project took people into the forest to see the damage for themselves, and hunter Wiremu Wharepapa, who has roamed the range since boyhood, calls it simply his backyard. The project hopes the forest's birdsong, now sparse, will begin to return.

stories.headline: Hundreds of Critically Endangered Canterbury Knobbled Weevils Released After Lab Breeding
stories.summary: Six weevils bred in a Mosgiel lab produced 260 offspring, and about 215 have been released into Canterbury's foothills. The species was once thought extinct.
stories.narrative:
One of New Zealand's most threatened insects has been given a boost. The Department of Conservation has released about 215 Canterbury knobbled weevils at a secret location in the Canterbury foothills.

The weevil was once thought extinct before it was rediscovered in the early 2000s. In a laboratory in Mosgiel, just six founding weevils produced 260 offspring, a result DOC entomologist Tara Murray said the team was delighted with.

The insects were placed in small cages over speargrass, their preferred host plant, in a gentle soft release. They burrow to the base of the plants, and the cages come off after a week or two. Owls were once their main predator, but introduced hedgehogs and rodents are now the greatest danger, so the site was chosen with care.

stories.headline: Namibia's Lion Rangers Use Smartphones and Ancient Tracking Skills to Protect Desert Lions
stories.summary: A community programme across 11 conservancies in north-west Namibia combines GPS collars and phone software with traditional tracking, and has eliminated illegal lion killings in six conservancies.
stories.narrative:
In Namibia's Kunene region, a community-run programme called Lion Rangers is helping people live alongside desert lions. It covers about 40,000 square kilometres across 11 conservancies, from the Skeleton Coast to the edge of Etosha.

It started in 2018 after farmer Benjamin Kordom's family farm was visited by lions that took poultry. He joined the programme and is now its field coordinator, overseeing more than 40 rangers who track lions on foot using skills handed down through generations, alongside a free app called SMART, camera traps, and GPS collars on 44 lions.

Early-warning towers with sirens and spotlights guard conflict hotspots, and text alerts tell rangers when collared lions cross virtual fences. The lion population has fallen to about 60, which the programme considers stable, as prey declined sharply. Illegal lion killings have been eliminated in six conservancies.

Conflict incidents have crept up recently as weather shifts push lions into new areas, and the story is honest about that. But Kordom, who rebuilt his own herd after drought, sums up the approach: let's try to live together with these lions.

stories.headline: Scientists Recreate the Colour-Changing Glass of the Roman Lycurgus Cup
stories.summary: A University of Sheffield team has reproduced the dichroic glass of the 4th-century Lycurgus Cup using Roman-era materials, closer to the original than earlier attempts. A replica will go on permanent display.
stories.narrative:
Researchers have recaptured a Roman secret that had been lost for about 1,600 years. The Lycurgus Cup, held at the British Museum, looks green in reflected light and glows red when light shines through it, thanks to tiny gold and silver nanoparticles embedded in the glass.

Lisa Hollands, a glass specialist at the University of Sheffield, led a team that first recreated Roman-style glass from materials available at the time, then spent a long period experimenting with oxygen levels and furnace temperatures. The colour turned out to depend heavily on where the glass sat in the furnace, which made it hard to control.

Ian Freestone of University College London suggested the Romans must have struggled too, and may have hit the jackpot with the cup. The new glass is a far closer match to the original than the version made by NASA in the 1960s. Glass artist Elliot Walker then used it to make an artwork, and the replica will be shown permanently at Sheffield's Turner Museum of Glass.

stories.headline: Six New Calves Lift a Sacred Mekong Irrawaddy Dolphin Population to 118
stories.summary: A stretch of the Mekong River in northeastern Cambodia recorded six dolphin calves in its latest breeding season, taking the local Irrawaddy dolphin population to 118. Local communities regard the animals as sacred, and conservation work there has run since 2014.
stories.narrative:
In northeastern Cambodia, a 75-mile stretch of the Mekong River has just had a good breeding season for one of Southeast Asia's most endangered freshwater mammals. Six Irrawaddy dolphin calves were born in the latest season, and that brings the local population up to 118 animals.

These dolphins live in a river under heavy pressure. Around 160 dams along the Mekong have changed parts of their habitat, and fishing nets have long been a danger to them. Every new calf that survives matters a great deal for a population this small.

The recovery has not happened by accident. Conservation groups, including the Cambodian arm of the World Wildlife Fund, began a joint programme with local people back in 2014. Communities in both Cambodia and neighbouring Laos regard the dolphins as sacred, and that cultural respect has been a foundation for the protection work.

Six calves is a modest number in absolute terms, but for a group of this size it is a meaningful gain, and a sign that years of patient work alongside riverside communities are paying off. It is a reminder that even in a river in crisis, a species can hold on and begin to grow again.

stories.headline: Boat Crew Rescues Exhausted Kangaroo Found Swimming Two Miles Off South Australia
stories.summary: A crew heading out from Port Lincoln spotted a juvenile kangaroo struggling in the water about 3 km offshore and turned back to haul it aboard. After a rest, the young roo hopped off the beach unharmed.
stories.narrative:
Off the coast of South Australia, a boat crew had an unusual rescue on their hands. While out in Boston Bay, near Port Lincoln, the skipper, Ryan Smith, noticed something in the water that turned out to be a young kangaroo, roughly three kilometres from land.

The crew turned the boat around to take a closer look. The sea was calm, so they lowered the boat's rear water door, and a farmer on board, Jake Murray, was able to scoop the tired animal out of the water. A scuba diver from the Galapagos Islands, Miguel Villarroel, was also aboard for the surprise.

The kangaroo was exhausted and spent part of the trip dozing in Murray's arms. Back on shore, hours later, it hopped off the beach under its own steam and headed away.

It is a small story, but a very warm one: a few people noticed an animal in trouble, changed their plans, and gave it a second chance.

stories.headline: New Certification Scheme Rewards Solar Farms That Become Havens for Wildlife
stories.summary: UK group Wild Power has launched a certification for renewable energy sites that meet biodiversity standards, and two solar farms have already been certified. One Essex site expects a 65% rise in habitat biodiversity units through wildflower grassland, hedgerow repairs and nest boxes.
stories.narrative:
A new scheme in the United Kingdom is aiming to make clean energy better for nature as well as the climate. Wild Power, an organisation founded in 2022, has launched a certification for renewable energy sites that meet biodiversity standards, and two UK solar farms have now earned it.

The idea grew from a co-founder's visit to a hillside solar farm in northern Spain, where animals grazed among wildflowers. Wild Power first thought of building such farms itself, but instead built a free scorecard that developers can use to measure and improve their sites. It looks at habitats, species, connections to surrounding land, monitoring and management, and sites scoring at least 70 points can apply for independent certification. Its director likens it to a fair trade stamp for clean energy.

The second certified site is Dunmow, a ten megawatt solar farm in Essex. Changes there include species-rich grassland, wildflower areas, repaired hedgerows, bird and bat boxes, and scrub cleared near a skylark area. The owners project a 65 percent increase in habitat biodiversity units, though those gains will take years to fully mature.

With the UK aiming to roughly double its solar capacity by 2030, and a survey suggesting half of renewable customers would pay extra for electricity from high-biodiversity sites, this approach could help make the energy transition good for wildlife too.

stories.headline: Daily Fibre Supplement Eased Knee Arthritis Pain and Boosted Grip Strength in Trial
stories.summary: In a randomised trial of 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis, the prebiotic fibre inulin reduced knee pain and improved grip strength within six weeks. University of Nottingham researchers say larger studies are needed, but it points to a cheap, simple option.
stories.narrative:
Researchers at the University of Nottingham have reported encouraging results from a trial of a simple fibre supplement for people with knee osteoarthritis. The six-week study, called INSPIRE, involved 117 adults and compared inulin, a prebiotic fibre found in foods like chicory root, with digitally supported physical therapy, both together, and a placebo.

Both inulin and physical therapy reduced knee pain on their own. Inulin also improved grip strength and lowered pain sensitivity, benefits not seen with physical therapy alone. People taking inulin were also far more likely to stick with the trial, with about 4 percent dropping out compared with 21 percent in the physical therapy group.

The team found the supplement raised levels of butyrate, a gut-produced compound, and better grip strength was linked to higher levels of a hormone called GLP-1, hinting at a gut-to-joint connection.

The authors are careful to say the trial was small and short, and that fibre should not replace exercise or established treatments. Still, it is a hopeful early sign that an inexpensive, easy-to-take supplement could help the millions living with arthritis pain.

stories.headline: Cancer Drug Cuts Risk of Progression by 41% in Women With Recurrent Endometrial Cancer
stories.summary: A phase 3 trial of 776 women whose endometrial cancer had returned after immunotherapy found the antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab tirumotecan lowered the risk of progression by 41% and of death by 32% compared with standard chemotherapy. Tumours shrank in 35% of patients on the new drug versus 17% on chemotherapy. Results were presented at ESMO and published in The Lancet.
stories.narrative:
Women whose womb cancer comes back after immunotherapy have had few good options, and chemotherapy has long been the fallback. A large international trial presented this week suggests there may now be something better.

The study, led from NYU Langone's Perlmutter Cancer Center and run at more than two hundred cancer centres in twenty-nine countries, compared a newer drug called sacituzumab tirumotecan with chemotherapy chosen by each patient's doctor. The drug is an antibody-drug conjugate: it homes in on a protein found on many tumour cells and delivers a toxic payload directly to them. Everyone enrolled had advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer and had already been treated with pembrolizumab.

In total, 386 women received the new drug and 390 received chemotherapy. Those on the new drug had a 41 percent lower risk of their disease progressing, and a 32 percent lower risk of dying. Tumours shrank in just over a third of women on the new treatment, roughly double the rate seen with chemotherapy. The side effects, including low blood counts, mouth sores and dry or itchy eyes, were described by the researchers as manageable.

The lead investigator said the results point to a new standard of care for this group of patients. The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress and published at the same time in The Lancet.

There are caveats worth hearing. The trial was open-label, it was funded by the drug's manufacturer, and the drug is not yet approved. But a randomised trial this large showing both slower progression and longer survival is exactly the kind of result that changes treatment, and it gives women facing a returning cancer a real prospect of more time.

stories.headline: Forest Staff Spend Seven Hours Tracking Down a Mother Elephant to Reunite Her With Her Rescued Calf
stories.summary: A mother elephant and her calf fell into a water tank in Kurseong, West Bengal, and forest staff pulled both out, but the calf was separated from the herd in the process. The team followed the mother through the forest for seven hours until they could bring the pair back together.
stories.narrative:
In Kurseong, in the hills of West Bengal, a mother elephant and her calf tumbled into a water tank. Forest department staff got both animals out safely, but in the confusion of the rescue the calf ended up separated from its mother, which can be a death sentence for a young elephant.

Instead of leaving the calf to fend for itself, the Kurseong forest team set out to find the mother. For about seven hours they tracked her through the surrounding forest, while the calf waited under their care.

When they finally located her, the staff released the calf. Video shared by Indian Forest Service officer Parveen Kaswan on 25 October shows the mother coming back, rejoining her herd and leading her calf away with her. Kaswan praised the team's persistence.

It is a small story, but a satisfying one: two animals saved from a water tank, and a family put back together because a group of people refused to give up halfway through the job.

stories.headline: Auckland Lecturer Who Took Up Taekwon-Do With Her Daughter Wins World Cup Gold
stories.summary: Dr Jean Uasike Allen, a University of Auckland senior lecturer, won her division at the ITF Taekwon-Do World Cup in Spain just four years after starting the sport with her shy teenage daughter. She had taken silver at the previous World Cup in Argentina.
stories.narrative:
Dr Jean Uasike Allen had never done any martial arts when her teenage daughter Layla asked to join a Taekwon-Do club in 2022 but felt too shy to go alone. So Jean joined too, and she has not looked back.

This month, the University of Auckland senior lecturer, who researches and teaches sport and physical education, won gold in the women's 36 to 45 patterns division at the ITF Taekwon-Do World Cup in Benidorm, Spain, representing New Zealand. At the previous World Cup in Argentina she had come second, so the gold was a step up.

She described the win as surreal, and said she could hear the whole New Zealand team and supporters cheering for her. She also enjoys being an unconventional competitor, older and larger than the typical martial artist, and says there is something a little disruptive in that.

Beyond the medal, she says the best part has been the friendships made at home and overseas. It is a heartening story of a parent supporting a child's first step and ending up a world champion herself.

stories.headline: Passer-By With No Medical Training Leaps Onto Runaway School Bus and Stops It After Driver Has a Seizure
stories.summary: A 27-year-old man outside a St. Paul shop saw a school bus rolling after its driver appeared to have a seizure. He jumped aboard, pulled the parking brake and stayed with the driver until paramedics arrived. All 18 students on board were safe.
stories.narrative:
In St. Paul, Minnesota, a quiet break from work turned into a rescue. Ebro Ahmed, who is 27, was outside a snack shop in the Dayton's Bluff neighbourhood when he noticed a middle school bus still moving with no one in control.

The driver appeared to have had a seizure. There were 18 students from Battle Creek Middle School on board. Ahmed ran toward the bus, jumped through the open doors and pulled the parking brake, bringing it to a stop.

He then called police and stayed beside the driver until paramedics arrived. Ahmed has no medical training. He says he kept his head by drawing on what he had seen in TV medical dramas. The whole thing was caught on the shop's security camera.

No children were hurt. Ahmed was given a thousand-dollar reward for what he did. It is a reminder that ordinary people, in a moment's decision, can be the difference between a frightening incident and a disaster.

stories.headline: Five Cheetah Cubs Born at Smithsonian Facility Can Be Watched Live on Cheetah Cam
stories.summary: A cheetah named Zura gave birth to five cubs on October 5 at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute in Virginia. A live webcam lets the public watch the family around the clock, while staff monitor them with minimal disturbance. Only about 7,000 cheetahs remain in the wild.
stories.narrative:
At the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Virginia, a cheetah named Zura gave birth to five cubs on the fifth of October.

A live Cheetah Cam is now streaming from the den, so anyone can watch the mother nursing, grooming and playing with her cubs, day and night. Caretakers use the same camera feed to keep an eye on the family from a distance.

That matters for the cubs. With less early human contact than cubs in a typical zoo, they can bond more fully with their mother, and researchers can study natural behaviour that would be hard to observe otherwise.

Cheetahs are vulnerable, with only around 7,000 left in the wild, so a healthy litter of five is welcome news for the species.

stories.headline: FDA Approves Immunotherapy Alone for Some Rectal Cancers, Letting Patients Skip Surgery, Radiation and Chemo
stories.summary: The FDA has approved dostarlimab (Jemperli) as a standalone treatment for stage 2 and 3 rectal cancers with a specific genetic signature. In the AZUR-1 trial, nearly three in four patients showed no sign of cancer a year after finishing six months of treatment. Side effects were generally mild.
stories.narrative:
Some people with rectal cancer may now be able to avoid surgery, radiation and chemotherapy altogether. The US Food and Drug Administration has approved the immunotherapy drug dostarlimab, sold as Jemperli, as the sole treatment for stage two and three rectal cancers that carry a particular genetic feature known as mismatch repair deficiency.

The approval rests on interim results from the AZUR-1 trial, which enrolled more than 150 patients in ten countries. They received the drug every three weeks for six months. Nearly three in four showed no sign of cancer a year after finishing, and no recurrences have been reported among those who responded, with more than half followed for over two years.

Side effects were mostly mild, such as fatigue, rash, diarrhoea and itchy skin, a stark contrast to the life-altering effects of rectal surgery and radiation.

The tumour type affects roughly five to ten percent of rectal cancer patients. Doctors caution that an independent FDA review saw a lower figure, around half, and that longer follow-up is needed. Even so, it is a major step toward gentler cancer care.

stories.headline: Endangered Southern Resident Orca J35 Welcomes a New Healthy Calf
stories.summary: Researchers spotted a new male calf, designated J65, with orca J35 on October 19. He appears healthy, moving well and nursing. It is a hopeful sign for an endangered population whose mother has endured heartbreaking losses.
stories.narrative:
A new calf has been born into the endangered Southern Resident killer whale community of the Pacific Northwest. The Center for Whale Research first saw him on October 19, swimming beside his mother J35 and estimated to be less than a week old.

Drone footage the next day confirmed he is male. He has been named J65. Researchers saw no health problems, and he was moving well, socialising and nursing.

J35 is a well-known whale. In 2018 she carried a dead calf for seventeen days in what became known as the Tour of Grief. A daughter born in 2024 did not survive. J65 is her fifth documented calf.

About half of Southern Resident calves survive their first year, so scientists are cautious, but every healthy birth matters for a population this small.

stories.headline: Zoo Vets in Amsterdam Fit a Hornbill With a 3D-Printed Beak in a World First
stories.summary: A southern ground hornbill at ARTIS Royal Zoo broke both halves of its beak, and vets fitted it with two 3D-printed prostheses. The bird was using the new beak within hours and eating on its own the same day.
stories.narrative:
At ARTIS Royal Zoo in Amsterdam, a male southern ground hornbill suffered a serious injury: both the upper and lower parts of his beak broke, leaving two misshapen stumps. For a bird that relies on its beak to pick up food, that could have been a life-threatening problem.

Zoo veterinarian Martine van Zijll Langhout teamed up with the veterinary faculty at Utrecht University to find a fix. CT scans of the bird's skull guided the design of two custom prostheses, which were 3D-printed in plastic.

The new beak parts were attached using titanium components and screws. Within hours of the operation, the hornbill was already using his new beak. The next morning he picked a mouse up off the ground, and later that day he was eating by himself.

The team says that, as far as they could find in the scientific literature, nobody has previously replaced both the upper and lower parts of a bird's beak this way. Long-term results are still unknown, but the early signs are encouraging, and the technique could help other birds with similar injuries.

stories.headline: Brazil's Amazon Deforestation Falls to the Lowest Level Since Records Began
stories.summary: Brazil's space agency reports 3,335 square kilometres of Amazon forest cleared in the year to July, 42% less than the year before and the lowest since records began in 1988. Clearing in the Cerrado savanna also hit a record low.
stories.narrative:
Brazil has recorded the smallest amount of Amazon deforestation since satellite monitoring began in 1988. The national space agency, Inpe, says about 3,335 square kilometres of forest were cleared in the twelve months to July, roughly 42 percent less than the year before.
